summary: This standards-track memo defines MIB objects for SNMP management of Multimedia Terminal Adapters in PacketCable and IPCablecom systems. It was later updated by RFC 9141.

eli5.summary: A multimedia terminal adapter lets an ordinary phone work over a cable network. This gives operators a list of dials and gauges to check on these adapters from far away.

subtitle: The SNMP MIB that lets cable operators inspect and control PacketCable and IPCablecom voice adapters.

tldr.problem: Cable operators who offer voice over IP need a standard way to manage the Multimedia Terminal Adapters (MTAs) that connect ordinary phones to the cable network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the PKTC-IETF-MTA-MIB module, rooted at pktcIetfMtaMib, with three object groups for the device itself, its provisioning servers and its security setup, plus two provisioning notifications.
tldr.outcome: SNMP managers get one IETF-defined set of objects for MTAs. Many writable objects are sensitive, so the RFC urges strong SNMP security. RFC 9141 later updated this document.

today: RFC 4682 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, and it was updated by RFC 9141.

sections.title: What the MTA MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 4682 defines a MIB module, a set of managed objects accessed with SNMP, for devices that comply with PacketCable, ETSI and ITU-T IPCablecom requirements. It is intended to supersede several earlier MTA MIB modules from which it is partly derived: the PacketCable 1.0 MTA MIB, the ITU-T IPCablecom MTA MIB requirements and the ETSI MTA MIB.

Where PacketCable and IPCablecom requirements are equivalent, the PacketCable reference is used in each object's REFERENCE clause, and IPCablecom devices MUST use the equivalent IPCablecom references. The module is written in SMIv2.
sections.eli5: This is a big checklist of things an operator can look at or change on a phone adapter, written so that any management tool can read it.

sections.title: Devices and Terms
sections.content:
A Multimedia Terminal Adapter (MTA) is a PacketCable- or IPCablecom-compliant device that provides telephony over a cable system. It has an interface to endpoints, a network interface, CODECs, and the signaling functions needed for Voice over IP, call signaling and Quality of Service signaling. An Embedded MTA (E-MTA) contains a DOCSIS cable modem. A Standalone MTA (S-MTA) is separated from the cable modem by a non-DOCSIS interface such as Ethernet or USB.

An endpoint is a standard RJ-11 telephony port on the MTA. Other parties in the picture are the Call Management Server (CMS), which controls audio connections between MTAs, the Operations Systems Support (OSS) back office, and the Key Distribution Center (KDC), a Kerberos security server that provides mutual authentication of PacketCable components.
sections.eli5: The adapter is a little box with a phone jack. Some boxes are built into the cable modem, and some sit beside it. Other servers in the company set it up and keep it safe.

sections.title: Structure of the Module
sections.content:
The module is identified as pktcIetfMtaMib, placed at { mib-2 140 }. Its objects fall into three groups. pktcMtaDevBase covers the MTA device itself, pktcMtaDevServer covers the provisioning back office servers, and pktcMtaDevSecurity covers the PacketCable and IPCablecom security mechanisms. The module also has a pktcMtaDevErrors branch and a conformance section.

The first two groups hold only scalar objects. The security group holds two tables, the realm table and the CMS table, that control the associations between KDC realms and application servers. Table rows can be created automatically by the device or by the management station, so a table may contain both kinds.

The module supports a single Provisioning Server.
sections.eli5: The checklist has three chapters: one about the box, one about the servers that set it up, and one about its locks and keys.

sections.title: Key Objects
sections.content:
In the base group, pktcMtaDevSerialNumber holds the serial number and pktcMtaDevEndPntCount the number of endpoints. pktcMtaDevProvisioningState reports how the initialization process finished. pktcMtaDevEnabled lets an operator enable or disable telephony services, and setting pktcMtaDevResetNow to true makes the device reset immediately. A reset flushes connections, ends current actions such as ringing, disables all endpoints and restarts the provisioning flow at step MTA-1.

In the server group, objects hold the addresses of the primary and secondary DHCP and DNS servers, and pktcMtaDevConfigFile names the configuration file the MTA must download from the Provisioning Server. pktcMtaDevProvConfigHash holds a hash of that file's content, which the MTA uses to authenticate the file after download.

A textual convention lists the algorithms usable to encrypt the configuration file, from none(0) to aes256CbcMode(4).
sections.eli5: Some items are gauges you can only read, like the serial number. Others are switches, like turning the phone service on or off or restarting the box.

sections.title: Security Associations and Certificates
sections.content:
An MTA talks to two kinds of back office application servers: Call Management Servers and Provisioning Servers. Setting up a Security Association with them takes two steps defined in the PacketCable Security Specification. The first is the Authentication Server exchange (AS-exchange), which authenticates both sides and uses parameters grouped per realm in pktcMtaDevRealmTable. The second is the application server exchange (AP-exchange), which establishes the association between authenticated parties and uses pktcMtaDevCmsTable, indexed by an index counter and holding each CMS's FQDN and Kerberos realm name.

E-MTAs must use X.509 certificate based authentication, and pktcMtaDevRealmOrgName should contain the organization name attribute of the Telephony Service Provider certificate. For secure software download, E-MTAs are upgraded by the cable modem under DOCSIS rules, while S-MTAs implement a specific mechanism using Code Verification Certificates.
sections.eli5: Before the box and a server trust each other, they show proof of who they are, like two people showing ID before swapping keys.

sections.title: Provisioning State and Notifications
sections.content:
The module defines two INFORM notifications. pktcMtaDevProvisioningEnrollment is issued by the MTA to start PacketCable provisioning when SNMP enrollment is used. It carries the system description, software version, device type identifier, MAC address and a correlation ID. pktcMtaDevProvisioningStatus may be issued by the MTA to confirm that provisioning is complete and to report the result, along with the MAC address and correlation ID.

The result is the pktcMtaDevProvisioningState value, such as pass, inProgress or failConfigFileError. Seven values are defined in total.
sections.eli5: The box can send a message saying "I am here, please set me up" and later another saying "I finished, and it worked" or "it did not".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Many objects are read-write or read-create, and setting them without protection can disrupt service. Setting pktcMtaDevResetNow or pktcMtaDevEnabled maliciously would reset the device or stop its service. All writable objects in the server group and some in the realm table could prevent proper provisioning, and writable CMS table objects could change which Call Management Server the MTA registers with.

Readable objects can also be sensitive. The server addresses and certificate objects could help attackers launch denial-of-service attacks against provisioning or Kerberos servers, and pktcMtaDevFQDN may reveal domain topology. The RFC notes that SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and that even on a secure network there is no control over who may read or change these objects. Implementers are RECOMMENDED to consider the available security features.
sections.eli5: Some switches on the box can break phone service if the wrong person flips them. So only trusted people should be allowed to look at or change them.
